opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to do both, honestly, and the trick is in how you sequence them. Everyone in this field dreams of the big one: the room-temperature superconductor, a sorbent that pulls CO2 out of the air at a fraction of today's cost, a battery chemistry that changes everything. Those are the moonshots, and they're the reason many of us got into this. But if you only chase moonshots, you can go a very long time without anything to show for it, and in the meantime you aren't learning whether your tools actually work in the real world.

So the way I think about it is that the modest goals with companies are not a distraction from the breakthrough. They're the path to it. When you work with an industrial partner on a concrete problem, say they need a slightly better material for a specific separation process or a coating with certain properties, you get real constraints, real data, and real feedback from the lab. You find out where your models are overconfident, where the simulations don't match experiment, and where synthesizability kills an otherwise beautiful candidate. That's incredibly valuable, and you can't get it from benchmarks.

It also builds the engine. What we're really building is a search engine for materials: generative models, fast surrogate models for the physics, and eventually closed-loop experimentation. Every incremental project makes that engine better. If the engine gets good enough, the breakthroughs become much more likely, almost a byproduct of running it at scale on the right problems.

There's also a practical side. Companies need to see value on a reasonable timescale, and so do the people funding this work. Delivering on smaller, well-defined problems earns you the trust and the resources to take bigger swings. And I'd say the climate problem, which is what motivates me most, doesn't give us the luxury of waiting twenty years for a single miracle material. A lot of good, deployable 10 or 20 percent improvements across many processes add up.

So keep the North Star in view, the materials that could genuinely change our trajectory on energy and climate, but walk toward it through a series of concrete, useful steps with partners who keep you honest.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a tension we live with every day at CuspAI, honestly. Let me try to be candid about it.

The thing that got me to leave the comfortable academic world and start a company was the big bet: can we actually use generative models and simulation to discover materials that matter for climate? Carbon capture sorbents, better catalysts, battery components, that kind of thing. If you pull that off, the impact is enormous. But it's also slow, it's uncertain, and the validation loop runs through a wet lab, not through a benchmark. You can't just scale compute and get a result in a week. Synthesis and characterization take months, and the chemistry fights you.

So if you only chased the moonshot, you'd be a research lab burning money with no feedback from the world for years. And I actually think that's dangerous, not just financially but scientifically. You lose touch with what the real constraints are. A material that looks perfect in silico might be unsynthesizable, or too expensive, or degrade after fifty cycles. The companies that make and use these materials know that. We don't, unless we talk to them.

The way I think about it is that the more modest engagements are not a distraction from the big goal. They are the training data, in a sense. When a partner comes to us and says, we need a sorbent with these properties under these conditions, that forces us to confront the full pipeline. Generation, screening, stability prediction, synthesizability. Every one of those shorter projects tells us where our models are wrong. And that's exactly what you need if you're eventually going to make the ambitious discovery.

There's also a cultural thing. If you hire great scientists and tell them the payoff is seven years away, a lot of them will drift. If they can see something they built actually getting tested in a lab, or a partner actually caring about the result, that keeps people honest and motivated.

Where I draw the line is this: we don't take on work that pulls us off the platform we're building. If a company wants pure consulting, essentially "run your tools for us on our problem," and it doesn't improve our models or our understanding, we say no, even if the money is good. Every project has to feed the flywheel. The question I ask is, will we be better at discovery after doing this than before? If yes, we do it. If it's just revenue, we don't.

And I'll admit there's some faith involved. I come from machine learning, where we've seen this pattern before. The grand ambition in deep learning was there for decades, but it got built on a lot of unglamorous incremental work and real applications. I think materials will go the same way. The breakthrough won't come from a single heroic effort. It'll come from a system that's been ground against reality a few hundred times. So I'd rather be modest and useful in the near term, as long as every modest thing we do is pointed at the same horizon.

astra-6.text:
I think you need a balance. A major materials breakthrough is exciting, and you want to leave room for ideas that might take a long time or might not work. But working with companies on more modest goals gives you concrete constraints: what actually needs to improve, what can be measured, and what would make a difference in practice.

Those smaller goals can also teach you where the hard scientific problems are. So I wouldn’t treat the two as separate paths. You can make useful progress with a company while keeping a longer-term research question in view. The important thing is to be clear about which kind of effort you’re undertaking, because the expectations and timescales are very different.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need both. You want an ambitious goal, something that could really change the way we discover materials. But if everything depends on one enormous breakthrough, you can spend years working without finding out whether what you’re building is actually useful.

Working with companies gives you concrete problems and constraints. Can you improve a particular property? Can you reduce the number of experiments needed to find a promising material? Those may sound like more modest goals, but they force you to connect the machine learning to the actual science and to the experimental process.

So I would keep the big ambition as a direction, while looking for smaller steps that have value on their own. Ideally, what you learn from those steps also makes the bigger breakthrough more likely.
